terms.comment: Also a name; in the grammarians a noun, adjectives included. A proper noun is nōmen proprium, a common noun nōmen appellātīvum (Traupman 220, 248).

evidence: Varr. LL 8.11: ōrātiōnis duās partēs esse dīcit, vocābula et verba (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Varro’s word for the noun beside the verb; some grammarians kept nōmen for proper names and vocābulum for common nouns (Quint. 1.4.20).
Quintilian treats it, with vocābulum, as a kind of nōmen.

terms.gloss: a noun, as opposed to an adjective
evidence: M-O s.v. parts of speech: noun, after Vives
terms.comment: The later grammars’ term, which sets nouns apart from adjectives; substantīvus is late Latin (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Charis. p. 126 P.; Prisc. (Lewis & Short s.v. appellātīvus)

phrases.latin: veterēs enim … verba modo et nōmina et convīnctiōnēs trādidērunt; vidēlicet quod in verbīs vim sermōnis, in nōminibus māteriam (quia alterum est quod loquimur, alterum dē quō loquimur) … esse jūdicāvērunt
phrases.english: For the ancients handed down only verbs, nouns and conjunctions: they judged, that is, that the force of speech lies in the verbs and its matter in the nouns (since the one is what we say, the other what we speak about)

sources: Lewis & Short: nomen · Lewis & Short: vocabulum · Lewis & Short: appellatio · Lewis & Short: substantivus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. parts of speech: noun.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 220, 245, 247, 248, 294, 295.
